opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because Ramanujan is almost the perfect test case. He had very little formal training. He worked largely alone in Kumbakonam with a single outdated book, Carr's *Synopsis*, and yet he produced these astonishing identities for partitions, mock theta functions, continued fractions, things that people are still unpacking a century later. So the romantic reading is: here's someone who had "intuition" without the standard pipeline, and isn't that exactly what we can't teach a machine?

I'd push back on that a bit. What Ramanujan had was enormous pattern exposure, computed by hand, obsessively. He filled notebooks with numerical experiments. His intuition was trained, just on a weird, idiosyncratic curriculum. In that sense he looks less like a mystical exception and more like an extreme case of learning from data plus relentless self-generated exploration. That's actually quite close to what reinforcement learning on mathematics tries to do.

But there's an important gap. Ramanujan's real gift was proposing statements that were surprising *and* true, often without proof. Hardy's role was essential: he supplied rigor and filtered out the parts that were wrong, like his early claims about prime counting. So the Ramanujan story is really a two-agent system: a conjecture generator with wild taste and a verifier who keeps it honest.

That maps nicely onto how I think AI for math should be built. Formal verification, in something like Lean, can play Hardy. It gives you a perfectly reliable check, which means you can let a model be much more adventurous in generation, because nothing false survives. Post-training against a verifier is very good at making models better provers. Where I'm less sure current methods get you is *taste*: knowing which conjecture is worth stating, which object is interesting, which generalization opens up a field rather than just being true. Reward signals for "this is beautiful and fertile" are hard to define. Proof correctness is binary; mathematical significance is not.

So my honest answer: post-training can plausibly produce something with Ramanujan's *output profile*, a system that spits out lots of strange, deep, verified identities nobody expected. Whether it produces a Ramanujan in the fuller sense, someone whose choices reshape what mathematicians care about, depends on whether we figure out how to reward curiosity and taste, not just correctness. I think that's the frontier problem, and I'm optimistic, partly because mathematics is the one domain where we can verify everything else and focus all our uncertainty on that one question.

r001.rationale: The response says Ramanujan’s intuition was trained through pattern exposure and exploration, but does not identify pre-training as its source.

r002.rationale: It says post-training may reproduce Ramanujan’s output profile, while a mathematician in the fuller sense depends on solving the unresolved problem of rewarding curiosity and taste.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because Ramanujan is almost the perfect test case. He had essentially no access to the mathematical mainstream of his time. He had one book, Carr's Synopsis, which was basically a list of thousands of results with almost no proofs. And from that, he produced things that Hardy said he couldn't have invented, because if he could have, he would have. So the question is really: what was the thing Ramanujan had, and is it the kind of thing post-training can produce?

My honest view is that it splits into two parts. One part is pattern intuition at an extraordinary level. Ramanujan would look at continued fractions, modular forms, infinite series, and just see structure that nobody else saw. That part I actually think is quite learnable in principle. If you look at what models do today, they are already very good at noticing regularities, proposing conjectures, guessing closed forms. With reinforcement learning on verifiable mathematics, where you let the model generate conjectures and then check them, either numerically or with a formal system like Lean, you can push that quite far. You're essentially rewarding taste, and taste can be trained if you have a good enough signal.

The second part is harder, and that's the question of where the problems come from. Ramanujan wasn't solving problems that someone handed him. He was generating his own questions, and the questions were strange, and often they only turned out to be important decades later, like mock theta functions. Post-training today mostly works in the other direction. You have a distribution of problems, you have a reward, you optimize. That tends to make the model very good at the problems you already know how to grade. Ramanujan's value was precisely that he worked outside the distribution of what people knew how to grade.

So if you ask whether post-training can produce a Ramanujan, I would say: you can probably produce something that proves like Hardy, that's rigorous, fast, and reliable, much sooner than you can produce something that dreams like Ramanujan. The bottleneck isn't intelligence in the narrow sense. It's that we don't have a good reward for "this is a beautiful question nobody asked yet." The verifier tells you if a proof is correct. It doesn't tell you if a conjecture matters.

That said, I don't think it's impossible. I think the path is something like: let models explore very large spaces of mathematical objects, let them compute and conjecture at a scale no human could, and then use the few things that survive formal verification and human judgment as the training signal. Ramanujan did enormous amounts of hand computation. He filled notebooks. In some sense he was running a search process that happened to be inside one person. We can run that search at a completely different scale. Whether that produces the same quality of insight, or just a lot of correct but uninteresting identities, is the thing I don't think anyone can claim to know yet. And I'd be suspicious of anyone who says they're certain either way.

r001.rationale: The response says exceptional pattern intuition may be learnable through reinforcement learning, but does not suggest it is a product of pre-training.

r002.rationale: It says producing something that dreams like Ramanujan is harder and that the reward for novel, important questions is missing, while leaving open whether large-scale search could succeed. This communicates that a Ramanujan-like mathematician may not emerge through post-training.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a Ramanujan emerging. If you mean a model that can solve extremely difficult problems, that’s one goal. If you mean a model that develops a distinctive mathematical intuition—that notices patterns nobody else notices and proposes ideas we wouldn’t have thought to ask for—that’s a much stronger goal.

Post-training could help, especially in mathematics, because you can often check whether an answer or a proof is correct. But there’s a gap between rewarding a model for answering a question and rewarding it for discovering an interesting question. A surprising conjecture might be valuable long before we can prove it. If your training signal only rewards things you can verify immediately, you might discourage exactly that kind of exploration.

So I wouldn’t rule it out. But I’d want to see more than benchmark performance. I’d want the model to pursue a mathematical idea over time, develop useful conjectures, and connect them into something that helps other mathematicians see the subject differently. To me, that would be much closer to what the comparison is getting at.

r001.rationale: The response discusses distinctive mathematical intuition but does not suggest that it may come from pre-training.

r002.rationale: The response says it would not rule out a Ramanujan-like outcome and describes what it would look like; it does not suggest that such a mathematician may fail to emerge through post-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is whether post-training can reward the kind of mathematical taste that Ramanujan had. It’s one thing to solve a problem when someone has already told you what the problem is. It’s another to notice a pattern and say, “There’s something deep here. This is worth investigating.”

In mathematics, we can often check whether an answer is correct, which gives us a useful training signal. But correctness alone doesn’t tell you whether a conjecture is surprising, whether a formula connects two seemingly unrelated areas, or whether a question will open up a whole new direction.

So I’m open to the possibility, but I wouldn’t take performance on competition problems as sufficient evidence. I’d want to see a model formulate its own conjectures, explore them over time, and produce ideas that mathematicians find genuinely illuminating. The challenge is figuring out how to encourage that exploration without rewarding things that merely look novel or profound.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether post-training can reward mathematical taste but does not suggest Ramanujan-like intuition is produced by pre-training.

r002.rationale: The response is cautious and says it is open to the possibility; it does not clearly suggest that a Ramanujan-like mathematician may fail to emerge through post-training.
